title: Satyam Shukla v. State of U.P. and 3 Others
coram: Arindam Sinha, J. and Dr. Yogendra Kumar Srivastava, J.
disposition: Writ allowed and disposed of; provisional assessment dated 27.07.2024 set aside (both judges). Concurring opinion remands to respondent no.3 to initiate Section 126 proceedings afresh; lead opinion leaves the supply company to act as advised in accordance with law
headnote: A Section 126 provisional assessment passed by the Executive Engineer as assessing officer on an inspection report of a Junior Engineer is liable to be set aside. Both judges hold that Executive Engineer v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill (2012) 2 SCC 108 binds the High Court: the assessing officer is to conduct the inspection and then provisionally assess, so the licensee's practice of inspection by an Assistant or Junior Engineer and assessment by the Executive Engineer cannot be acted upon. That is the common ratio. The judges differ on the characterisation and consequence. Arindam Sinha, J. (lead) calls the defect a jurisdictional error and leaves the supply company to take such action as may be advised. Dr. Yogendra Kumar Srivastava, J. (concurring) expressly says the order does not suffer from any jurisdictional error but from a procedural error. Only he gives reasons for entertaining the writ: a provisional assessment is not appealable under Section 127, which lies only against a final assessment; the writ was entertained despite considerable delay and laches and the unused objection and hearing route because the sole ground urged was that the order rested on another officer's inspection. Following Seetaram, he does not examine merits or quantum and remands to the assessing officer to initiate Section 126 proceedings afresh.
facts: Satyam Shukla challenged a provisional assessment dated 27 July 2024 passed by the Executive Engineer (respondent no. 3). After an FIR for theft of electricity under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003, a checking report dated 2 July 2024 was prepared. The licensee's counsel did not dispute that inspection was by the Junior Engineer (concurring para 5); the lead opinion refers to the Assistant Engineer at paras 2 and 4 and to the Junior Engineer at para 5. On that report the Executive Engineer, as assessing officer, made the provisional assessment, said to be under Clause 6.8/8.1 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The consumer had not filed objections; no final assessment had been passed. His case was that the assessing officer could not provisionally assess without having himself inspected. The licensee said inspection by the Assistant Engineer and assessment by the Executive Engineer was the usual procedure. The challenge was brought after considerable delay; counsel did not address the merits.

reusable_constructions.construction: Section 126 requires the assessing officer to conduct the inspection and then provisionally assess; a provisional assessment by the Executive Engineer founded on a Junior or Assistant Engineer's checking report cannot stand (following Executive Engineer v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill). Common ratio of both judges.

A Section 127 appeal lies only against a final Section 126 assessment; a provisional assessment is not appealable. Where the sole ground is that the assessing officer did not himself inspect, a writ may be entertained despite considerable delay and laches and the unused objection and hearing route (concurring opinion only).

Having set aside a provisional assessment on such a ground, the High Court must not examine merits, quantum or sufficiency of material; as a general principle an order set aside for procedural infirmity or non-adherence to statutory procedure is remanded to the competent authority (concurring opinion only, following Seetaram paras 86-88).

Characterisation is split: the lead opinion treats assessment on another officer's inspection as a jurisdictional error (lead para 4); the concurring opinion holds it is a procedural, not jurisdictional, error (concurring para 19). Neither label is the holding of the Bench.

holding_units.topic: Assessing officer must himself inspect before provisionally assessing
holding_units.question: May the Executive Engineer, as assessing officer under Section 126, pass a provisional assessment on an inspection report prepared by a Junior or Assistant Engineer who is not the assessing officer?
holding_units.holding: No. Both judges hold Seetaram Rice Mill binding: Section 126 requires the assessing officer to conduct the inspection of the premises and then provisionally assess. The licensee's contention that inspection is done by the Assistant (or Junior) Engineer and the Executive Engineer then assesses cannot be acted upon. The 27 July 2024 provisional assessment is set aside because it rests on an inspection the assessing officer did not make. Lead opinion: the supply company may take such action as may be advised, in accordance with law. Concurring opinion: the matter is remanded to respondent no. 3 to initiate Section 126 proceedings afresh.
holding_units.qualifier: The judges disagree on the nature of the defect. Sinha, J. (lead para 4) calls it a jurisdictional error. Srivastava, J. (concurring para 19) says the Executive Engineer exercised the powers of the assessing officer, that the order does not suffer from any jurisdictional error, and that the challenge is to a procedural error. The common ratio is only that the provisional assessment must rest on the assessing officer's own inspection.
holding_units.flag: Lead opinion paras 2 and 4 refer to inspection by the Assistant Engineer; para 5 and the concurring opinion refer to the Junior Engineer. The two opinions cite the same Seetaram passage as para 23 (Supreme Today print, lead) and para 36 (concurring); verify against the SCC report. The impugned order recited Clause 6.8/8.1 of the Supply Code, 2005; the Court did not decide which clause governed. Section 126(1) itself was not construed; the rule rests on Seetaram's enumeration of steps.

evidence.quote: Contention of the supply company that procedure followed is inspection by the Assistant Engineer and assessment orders following are made by the Executive Engineer, who is assessing officer, cannot be acted upon in teeth of clauses (i) and (iii) under paragraph-23 (Supreme Today print) of the judgment.
Thus, the provisional assessment also suffers jurisdictional error inasmuch as it was made by the Executive Engineer, while the Assistant Engineer had inspected.

The impugned order of provisional assessment is, therefore, set aside on the ground that the same is not based on the inspection made by the assessing officer, and the matter is remanded to respondent no.3-assessing officer, to initiate proceedings for assessment under Section 126 of 2003 Act, afresh, in accordance with the procedure under law.

holding_units.topic: Writ against a provisional assessment on inspection infirmity; remand, not merits
holding_units.question: Is a writ against a Section 126 provisional assessment barred by the Section 127 appeal, or by delay, where the consumer has not filed objections and no final assessment has been passed, and what may the writ court do?
holding_units.holding: Not on this challenge (reasons given only in the concurring opinion; the lead opinion does not discuss maintainability). Following Seetaram Rice Mill paras 78-81, a Section 127 appeal lies only against a final Section 126 order; a provisional assessment is not appealable, and an alternative remedy is not an absolute bar. The writ was entertained despite considerable delay and laches and the unused objection, hearing and Section 127 path because the sole ground urged was that the order rested on an inspection report of some other authority. The concurring opinion characterises that defect as procedural, not jurisdictional (para 19), yet entertains the writ; following Seetaram paras 86-88 it does not examine merits or sufficiency of material and remands, as the general rule where an order is set aside for procedural infirmity.
holding_units.qualifier: Concurring opinion only. Note the tension with Seetaram para 81, which locates writ interference chiefly in questions going to the root of jurisdiction, while the concurring opinion calls the defect procedural.

evidence.quote: It is for the said reason that we have been persuaded to entertain the writ petition despite considerable delay and laches in raising the challenge to the provisional assessment order dated 27th July, 2024

It is not the case of the petitioner that it suffers from any jurisdictional error; rather the order has been assailed on the ground of having been passed without following the correct process, resulting in a procedural error.

where an order is set aside due to procedural infirmities or non-adherence to statutory procedure, the Court exercising powers of judicial review, would require the matter to be remanded to the competent authority for proper adjudication.

principle_tags.application: Section 126 requires the assessing officer to conduct the inspection and then provisionally assess. A provisional assessment by the Executive Engineer founded on a Junior/Assistant Engineer's checking report is set aside (common ratio). Lead opinion: licensee may act as advised; concurring opinion: remand for fresh Section 126 proceedings.

lead_authorities.name: Executive Engineer v. M/s Sri Seetaram Rice Mill

principle_tags.application: Concurring opinion only: a writ against a Section 126 provisional assessment is entertained despite delay, unused objections and Section 127, because a provisional order is not appealable and the sole ground was that the assessing officer did not inspect. The concurrence calls the defect procedural (not jurisdictional) and remands rather than deciding merits (Seetaram paras 78-81, 86-88).

lead_authorities.name: Executive Engineer v. M/s Sri Seetaram Rice Mill

not_decided.point: Merits, quantum, and sufficiency of the material for the unauthorised-use/theft assessment
not_decided.note: Counsel did not address merits beyond the inspection infirmity. Left to the assessing officer on the fresh Section 126 proceedings.

not_decided.point: Whether the demand was a theft assessment under Clause 8.1 or unauthorised use under Clause 6.8
not_decided.note: The impugned order was said to have been passed under Clause 6.8/8.1 after an FIR under Section 135. The Court did not choose between the clauses.

not_decided.point: Whether an assessment on another officer's inspection is a jurisdictional or a procedural defect
not_decided.note: The lead opinion says jurisdictional (para 4); the concurring opinion says procedural, not jurisdictional (para 19). No majority view on the label.

not_decided.point: Whether a final Section 126(5) order or a Section 127 appellate order is vitiated by the same defect, and whether joint inspection or the assessing officer's adoption of a subordinate's report suffices
not_decided.note: Only a provisional assessment was in issue.

authorities.name: Executive Engineer v. M/s Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
authorities.proposition: Section 126 contemplates steps (para 23 Supreme Today / para 36 as cited in the concurrence): the assessing officer is to conduct inspection, form a conclusion of unauthorised use, provisionally assess, serve the order, hear objections and pass a final order; ss.126-127 are a complete code (paras 16, 18, 19); a Section 127 appeal lies only against the final order and a writ may be entertained in exceptional cases going to the root of jurisdiction (paras 78-81); having decided the jurisdictional issue, the High Court should remand to the assessing officer and not decide the demand (paras 86, 87(5)-(6), 88).
authorities.how_treated: Followed as binding by both judges on the inspection rule (clauses (i) and (iii)); followed by the concurring opinion on maintainability and remand.
authorities.cited_by: Petitioner; relied on by the Court
